podcast.body: Initially considered a "throwaway" song by The Clash, it was intended as a free flexi-disc insert for NME magazine. When the NME deal failed, it was hastily added as an unlisted bonus track to their *London Calling* album. Despite its inauspicious origins, "Train in Vain" unexpectedly became the band's most commercially successful track. "this song, which was initially a throwaway, ended up becoming the clash's most commercially successful track."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This is an unlisted 19th song that appears at the end of side four of *London Calling*. It was not included on the original sleeve or labels because by the time it was recorded, the cover and labels had already been printed. The Clash managed to get it onto the acetate just before the vinyl was printed. The band had originally intended to release it for free as a flexi-disc with the *New Musical Express*, but the publisher refused, leading them to stick it onto the end of *London Calling*. It unexpectedly became an "honest to god top 40 hit" for the band.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was written and recorded rapidly at the conclusion of the "London Calling" recording sessions. Initially, the band intended to distribute it for free within the pages of a British music magazine, but when the magazine decided against it, The Clash simply included it on the album. Due to the album artwork already being finalized and sleeves printed, the song received no official mention, yet it was later discovered by audiences and went on to become a significant Top 40 hit in America. "But because the artwork had already been completed and albums sleeves that already been printed, there was no mention of the song. Didn't matter to the clash. Especially after it was discovered and became a big top 40 hit in America."
